prime.problem: The papers behind reasoning models come from different years and labs (InstructGPT, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, STaR, DeepSeek-R1) and it's easy to lose which ones train the model and which only change how it's used. This card puts them on one page, so each later card has a place to land.
prime.fits: The map for the course: read it first to see the four stages, or last as a recap. It builds on the hub's next-token language model cards and points to the card and study-path day for each stage.
expect: SFT, reward model, RLHF and DPO
inference-time compute: chain-of-thought, voting, step graders, "Wait"
RL with rule-checked rewards: STaR, GRPO, R1
the two levers: change the weights or spend tokens per question
prime.goal: Place any method from the course on one of the four stages, say whether it changes the weights or only spends more tokens at answer time, and name the card and day that teaches it.

attend: Why does the base model answer the apples question with another question, and which stage fixes that?
Which stages change the model's weights, and which one leaves them frozen?
What does each stage leave unsolved that the next stage goes after?
In the R1-Zero bars, which jump comes from training and which from voting?
Why does stage 4 only work on questions a rule can check?

must: Pretraining only teaches next-token prediction → the base model continues the page instead of answering → SFT on written answers and preference training (RLHF or DPO) turn it into an assistant

An assistant trained on what people prefer learns what they like, not what is right → a confident wrong answer can still score well → reasoning needs either more thinking at answer time or a reward that checks correctness

Inference-time methods (CoT, voting, step graders, "Wait") keep the weights fixed → every question costs more tokens and gains flatten → training-time methods (STaR, GRPO) pay once and every later answer benefits

A rule can check a maths or code answer but not an essay → rule-checked rewards can't be flattered, so large-scale RL works there → R1-Zero went from 15.6% to 71.0% on AIME 2024 with RL, and a vote of 64 took the same model to 86.7%

compress.prompt: Close the card and draw the four stages left to right. Under each, write what it does to the apples question and the one problem it leaves. Then mark which stages change the weights.
checklist: pretrain: next-token prediction → base model that continues text
assistant: SFT → reward model from preferences → RL, or DPO without the reward model
think at inference: CoT, sample and vote, step grader, "Wait"; same weights, more tokens
learn to think with RL: STaR and GRPO on rule-checked answers → R1
stages 1, 2 and 4 change the weights; stage 3 doesn't, and the two levers stack

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between the inference-time lever and the training-time lever in terms of when you pay and what changes.
answer: inference-time: weights fixed, more tokens or tries on every question
training-time: weights change once, up front
they stack: a trained reasoning model can still be voted

retrieve.q: Walk the apples question through all four stages: what does the model produce at each one, and what made the difference?
answer: base model: keeps writing the page
assistant: answers, but can be confidently wrong
inference: writes the steps, samples several, the vote gives 9
RL-trained: thinks in tags, re-checks, a rule rewards the right answer

retrieve.q: You have a fixed budget and a model that gets maths questions right about half the time. Argue for spending it on inference-time compute or on an RL run, and name what you give up.
answer: inference-time needs no training run and helps right away
but you pay per question, and gains flatten
RL costs a run and needs checkable answers, but every later answer benefits
high query volume favours training; a few hard questions favour inference

compare.q: Self-consistency and GRPO both sample many answers to one question. What does each do with the samples, and which lever is each?
answer: self-consistency votes and returns the most common answer; inference-time
GRPO scores each sample against the group mean and updates the weights; training-time
R1-Zero's 86.7% used both: GRPO training then a vote of 64

compare.q: RLHF and R1-Zero both run RL on a language model. What is different about where the reward comes from, and how does each fail?
answer: RLHF: a learned reward model trained on people's preferences
R1-Zero: a rule that checks the final answer and the format
a learned reward can be gamed, so RLHF needs a KL leash
a rule reward only exists for checkable tasks

predict.q: R1-Zero's one-try score was 71.0% and its vote of 64 was 86.7%. If you voted over 64 tries of the model at the start of RL (15.6% one try), would you expect to reach about 86.7%? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: No. Voting only helps when the right answer is the most common one among the samples. At 15.6% one-try accuracy the right answer is usually a minority, so the vote mostly picks a common wrong answer. The card doesn't give that number; the point is that voting amplifies what training put there.
